Title: Rome in World Time, Part 3: Carthage, Hannibal, and the Mediterranean (264–146 BC)

Summary: In 118 years Rome went from an Italian power to master of the Mediterranean: three wars with Carthage, Hannibal's invasion of Italy, wars against the kings of Macedon and Syria, and brutal fighting in Spain, ending with the destruction of both Carthage and Corinth in 146 BC. At the same time Qin unified China, the Han dynasty was founded in the same year as the Battle of Zama, Ashoka ruled India, and the Maccabees revolted in Judea.

---

This is the era when Rome became an empire in everything but name. The Greek historian **Polybius**, who lived through the end of it as a hostage in Rome, wrote his whole history to answer one question: how did the Romans conquer nearly the entire known world in under 53 years (220–167 BC)?

## The First Punic War (264–241 BC)

"Punic" comes from the Latin word for Phoenician, since Carthage was a Phoenician colony. The war started over Messana in Sicily and became a 23-year struggle for the island.

| Year (BC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 264 | Rome crosses to Sicily for the first time |
| 262 | Rome takes Agrigentum |
| 260 | **Mylae**: Rome, a land power, builds a fleet and wins its first naval battle using the *corvus*, a boarding bridge |
| 256 | Ecnomus, one of the largest naval battles of antiquity; Rome invades Africa under Regulus |
| 255 | Regulus defeated and captured by Carthage's Spartan mercenary general Xanthippus; a Roman fleet is wrecked by a storm |
| 249 | Drepana: consul Claudius Pulcher, told the sacred chickens would not eat, threw them overboard ("let them drink") and lost the battle |
| 247 | Hamilcar Barca, father of Hannibal, takes command in Sicily |
| 241 | **Aegates Islands**: Rome wins at sea; Carthage gives up Sicily, Rome's first province |

### Carthage's mutiny, Rome's opportunity

Right after the war, Carthage could not pay its mercenaries, and they revolted. The **Mercenary War** (241–237 BC), also called the Truceless War, was so savage that Polybius used it as a lesson in cruelty. While Carthage was distracted, Rome seized **Sardinia and Corsica** (238/237). The Carthaginians never forgave this.

### Between the wars

- 229–228 and 219 BC: Rome fights the **Illyrian** pirate kingdom of Queen Teuta, its first move across the Adriatic.
- 225 BC: Rome destroys a Gallic invasion at **Telamon**; 222 BC Marcellus kills a Gallic king in single combat at Clastidium.
- 237–219 BC: Hamilcar, then Hasdrubal, then **Hannibal** build a Carthaginian empire in Spain. In 219 Hannibal besieges Saguntum, a Roman ally.

## The Second Punic War: Hannibal (218–201 BC)

| Year (BC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 218 | Hannibal crosses the Pyrenees and the **Alps** with about 40,000 men and elephants; wins at the Trebia |
| 217 | **Lake Trasimene**: a Roman army is ambushed in fog. Fabius Maximus "the Delayer" adopts a strategy of avoiding battle |
| 216 | **Cannae**: Hannibal surrounds and destroys a Roman army of about 80,000. Perhaps 50,000 or more die in one afternoon |
| 216–215 | Capua and much of southern Italy defect to Hannibal; Philip V of Macedon allies with him (First Macedonian War, 214–205) |
| 213–211 | Siege of Syracuse; Archimedes' war machines delay Rome; he is killed in the sack (212) |
| 211 | Hannibal marches to the walls of Rome to draw Romans away from Capua. It fails; Capua falls. Both Scipio brothers are killed in Spain |
| 209 | The younger **Publius Cornelius Scipio**, aged about 25, captures New Carthage (Cartagena) |
| 207 | **Metaurus**: Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal is killed bringing reinforcements. His head is thrown into Hannibal's camp |
| 206 | Ilipa: Scipio drives Carthage out of Spain |
| 204 | Scipio invades Africa |
| 202 | **Zama**: Scipio defeats Hannibal |
| 201 | Peace: Carthage loses its fleet, Spain and its right to make war without Rome's permission |

### Mutiny and scandal inside Rome's army

- **206 BC, Sucro (Spain):** 8,000 of Scipio's soldiers mutinied over unpaid wages when a rumour said he was dead. Scipio recovered, invited them to assemble, surrounded them with loyal troops and executed 35 ringleaders (Livy 28.24–29).
- **205–204 BC, Locri:** Scipio's officer Pleminius plundered the allied city and even robbed its temple of Persephone. The scandal nearly cost Scipio his command.
- Rome also had to deal with defection from inside Italy: Capua, Tarentum and others joined Hannibal and were punished hard when retaken.

Around 211 BC Rome introduced the silver **denarius**, which became the backbone of its money for 450 years. In 204 BC, on the advice of a prophecy, Rome brought the **Magna Mater** (Cybele), an Anatolian goddess, into the city.

## Conquering the Greek East (200–146 BC)

| Years (BC) | War | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 200–196 | Second Macedonian War | 197: **Cynoscephalae**, the legion beats the Macedonian phalanx. 196: Flamininus declares the "freedom of the Greeks" |
| 192–188 | War with Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire | 191 Thermopylae, 190 **Magnesia**, 188 Peace of Apamea. Hannibal was serving as Antiochus' adviser |
| 183 | | Hannibal poisons himself in Bithynia rather than be handed to Rome; his rival Scipio dies the same year |
| 171–168 | Third Macedonian War | 168: **Pydna**. Macedon's monarchy is abolished |
| 168 | "Day of Eleusis" | The Roman envoy Popillius Laenas draws a circle in the sand around the Seleucid king Antiochus IV and demands he agree to leave Egypt before stepping out. He does |
| 167 | | Rome enslaves about 150,000 people in Epirus; 1,000 Achaean hostages, including Polybius, are taken to Italy |
| 149–148 | Fourth Macedonian War | The pretender **Andriscus** claims to be a son of the last king and raises Macedon in revolt |
| 146 | Achaean War | **Corinth** is destroyed by Mummius; Macedonia becomes a province |

## Spain: the endless war

Rome made two Spanish provinces in 197 BC and immediately faced revolts. The fighting lasted, on and off, for nearly two centuries.

- 197–195 BC: general revolt; Cato the Elder campaigns there.
- 181–179 BC: First Celtiberian War, ended with fair treaties by Tiberius Gracchus (father of the reformers).
- 154 BC onward: **Lusitanian** and **Celtiberian** wars. In 150 BC the governor Galba massacred Lusitanians who had surrendered.
- 147–139 BC: the shepherd-turned-general **Viriathus** led Lusitanian resistance and beat several Roman armies until Rome bribed his own men to murder him.
- The siege of **Numantia** ended in 133 BC (Part 4).

## The Third Punic War (149–146 BC)

Carthage had recovered economically and paid off its indemnity. **Cato the Elder** ended his speeches with "Carthage must be destroyed." When Carthage defended itself against the Numidian king Masinissa, Rome declared war, demanded Carthage give up its weapons (it did), then demanded the people abandon the city. They refused and held out for three years. In spring 146 BC **Scipio Aemilianus** took the city. It was burned, the survivors were sold into slavery, and the territory became the province of **Africa**. Polybius stood beside Scipio as Carthage burned and recorded that Scipio wept, thinking that Rome would one day share the same fate.

## Revolts and internal trouble in Rome

- **186 BC, the Bacchanalia affair:** the Senate violently suppressed the cult of Bacchus across Italy, claiming it was a conspiracy. Thousands were reportedly executed. A bronze copy of the decree survives.
- **Falerii (241 BC)** and **Capua (211 BC)** were Italian cities punished for revolt or defection.
- **Slave revolts:** a slave conspiracy in Latium (198 BC) and a large revolt in Apulia (185 BC) foreshadowed the great servile wars to come.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Zama and the Han dynasty: 202 BC.** The same year Scipio beat Hannibal, Liu Bang became emperor of a reunified China. Two of the most influential states in world history set their course in the same twelve months.

**Two great empires built at the same speed.** Qin unified China between 230 and 221 BC. Rome's leap from Italian power to Mediterranean master took 220 to 167 BC. Both were driven by states organised for war, and both had famously harsh ruling ideologies (Legalism in Qin, Cato-style austerity in Rome).

**The Rosetta Stone is a contemporary of Flamininus.** It was carved in 196 BC, the same year a Roman general stood up at the Isthmian Games and told the Greeks they were free.

**Rome befriended the Maccabees.** The Jewish revolt against the Seleucids (the origin of Hanukkah) happened while Rome was humiliating Seleucid kings. Rome and Judea signed a treaty in 161 BC. Two centuries later Rome would destroy the Temple.

**Ashoka and Rome were both conquering in the 260s.** Ashoka's Kalinga war and Rome's first fleet were near-simultaneous. Ashoka's remorse led to his rock edicts, which still survive across India. Rome felt no such remorse.

## What comes next

Part 4: Rome has no rivals left, so it turns on itself. The Gracchi brothers are killed, slaves revolt in Sicily, the Cimbri and Teutones destroy Roman armies, Italy's allies go to war with Rome, and Sulla marches his army on the city. Meanwhile, Emperor Wu of Han opens the Silk Road.

## Sources and notes

- Polybius, *Histories*. A near-contemporary and the best source for this period.
- Livy, *Ab Urbe Condita*, Books 21–45 (218–167 BC survive).
- Appian, *Roman History* (Punic, Iberian, Macedonian and Syrian books).
- Plutarch, *Lives* of Fabius Maximus, Marcellus, Flamininus, Cato the Elder, Aemilius Paullus.
- 1 Maccabees for the Judean events; Sima Qian, *Shiji*, for Qin and early Han; Ashoka's edicts (inscriptions).
- Adrian Goldsworthy, *The Fall of Carthage* (2000); Richard Miles, *Carthage Must Be Destroyed* (2010).
- Overview: [Punic Wars (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars), [Second Punic War (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War), [Macedonian Wars (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian_Wars).

**Flags:** Casualty figures for Cannae and Changping come from ancient writers and are probably inflated, especially the Chinese figure of 400,000 executed prisoners. The story that Rome sowed salt on Carthage's fields is a modern invention, not in any ancient source. The date of Ashoka's Kalinga war and the founding dates of Parthia and Bactria are approximate. El Mirador's peak dates are archaeological estimates.
